title: COP17: Developed countries ‘fall far short’ of UN targets for nature finance  - Carbon Brief
gist: A UN CBD stocktaking report says developed countries are failing to close the $200bn-per-year biodiversity finance gap: only $186.4bn was mobilised cumulatively in 2020-23 and just $17.7bn of international public finance, with the GBFF at under $400m and the Cali Fund at $6,000. Finance will be the most contested issue at COP17 in Armenia starting 19 October.

insights.claim: The UN CBD global stocktaking report finds countries mobilised a cumulative $186.4bn for biodiversity in 2020-23, under $50bn per year, which 'falls far short' of the $200bn-per-year target for 2030.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the gap that will drive COP17 finance negotiations.

insights.claim: Reporting countries raised only $17.7bn of international public biodiversity funding over 2020-23, about $4.4bn per year, so the milestone of at least $20bn per year by 2025 was 'likely not achieved'.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: A missed legally framed milestone strengthens developing-country demands for new finance mechanisms.

insights.claim: An OECD report puts global biodiversity finance at $74.9-92.4bn per year in 2023-2025, with international public finance averaging about $16.1bn per year, nearly $4bn below the 2025 goal.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Independent OECD data corroborate the UN's shortfall finding, reducing room for dispute over the numbers.
insights.locator: These figures are supported by a report from the OECD

insights.claim: Only $7.9bn in 2023 and $8.5bn in 2024 of the OECD-tracked finance was biodiversity-specific, with another $5.7bn and $6.5bn coming from funds where biodiversity was a secondary aim.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Headline finance totals overstate dedicated nature spending; discount mixed-purpose flows.

insights.claim: The GBF's $700bn finance gap splits into $500bn per year of harmful-subsidy reform (Target 18) and $200bn per year mobilised (Target 19), including at least $20bn per year of developed-to-developing public finance by 2025 and $30bn by 2030.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Useful decomposition of the commitments against which delivery will be judged.

insights.claim: The Global Biodiversity Framework Fund, housed under the GEF, received only $387.2m in signed commitments from 11 countries and Quebec between August 2023 and 30 June 2026, with only a handful of contributions after the pre-COP16 pledges.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Donor fatigue after an initial pledge flurry signals weak pipeline for dedicated nature funds.

insights.claim: The Cali Fund, the first global fund for companies profiting from genetic data, has received just two contributions totalling $6,000, against an LSE Grantham estimate that 21,690 eligible firms could raise $3.6bn annually, or $929m under realistic uptake.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Voluntary corporate contribution schemes are failing; the gap between potential and actual is several orders of magnitude.
insights.quote: the fund has received only two contributions, totalling $6,000

insights.claim: Voluntary corporate contribution to the Cali Fund is not working because no government has passed a law requiring companies to pay, and Cali Watch estimates eight companies alone should contribute more than $2bn.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Mandatory legislation is the likely route; watch for national laws on digital sequence information payments and exposure of named firms.

insights.claim: Dr Siva Thambisetty argues businesses will not shift on their own, because the private sector minimises outgoings and liability, so states with jurisdiction over business must act.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Regulatory pressure rather than voluntary appeals is the expected driver of corporate nature payments.
insights.quote: The private sector is doing what it always does: minimising outgoings and liability and maximising freedom to operate.

insights.claim: Third World Network's Lim Li Ching argues that developed countries have not met their legal obligations and that the failure should not be used as an excuse to pivot to private or market-based mechanisms, which struggle to raise finance at scale and often deepen social and ecological harm.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Developing-country bloc will resist offsets, carbon credits and debt-for-nature swaps as substitutes for public grants at COP17.
insights.quote: failure should not be used as an excuse to pivot to the private sector or market-based mechanisms

insights.claim: Debt-for-nature swaps, biodiversity offsets and carbon credits are the main private or innovative finance options but are harder to monitor and have often faced criticism.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Market-based nature instruments face scrutiny and credibility risk even as they are promoted to fill the gap.

insights.claim: Dr June Rubis warns that confidence in the wider biodiversity bargain erodes if one part of the finance architecture moves while the others (the $20bn commitment, predictable GBFF funding, Cali contributions, Cali allocation) are repeatedly deferred, and that Indigenous peoples need actual access to funds.
insights.speaker: Aruna Chandrasekhar
insights.so_what: Watch whether COP17 delivers coordinated, simultaneous signals across funders; access mechanics matter as much as headline pledges.
insights.quote: eadline commitments matter, but so do the pathways through which money reaches people
